historical_references.reference: Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah describes the Khilafat (Caliphate) of the Almohads (1121-1269 AD) in Al-Andalus (Iberian Peninsula) as a time of great political and cultural prosperity. The Almohads established a centralized government and promoted the study of Islamic sciences including mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy. The Islamic name 'Khali' may have originated during this period as a title for a high-ranking official or governor.

The name 'Khali' is also mentioned in the works of the Persian historian and poet, Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani, who lived during the Ghurid Empire (1148-1212 AD). He describes the Khilafat (Caliphate) of the Ghurids as a time of expansion and consolidation, during which the Caliphate's power extended over large parts of Afghanistan, Pakistan, and India. The term 'Khali' is used in Juzjani's works to refer to a high-ranking military officer or governor under the Ghurid Caliphate.
